games.predicted_reason: Eight-hour evening with a huge rulebook and ages of downtime, so my long playtime and heavy rulebook peeves make it a 1, like Brass.
games.actual_reason: The all-day playtime (5.5 to 7 hours even for groups needing rules reminders) is a major time commitment that a quick-game casual player would be unlikely to want to repeat, although downtime is reported as low.

games.predicted_reason: Giant rulebook, long setup and cleanup, and a bossy player running the co-op, so my heavy rulebook and setup peeves sink it.
games.actual_reason: Reviewers say outright that it is not a game for casual gamers because of the heavy setup, rulebook and 2-3 hour scenarios.

games.predicted_reason: A long engine builder with fiddly card icons and slow turns, which is exactly my 2 anchor and my downtime peeve.
games.actual_reason: Described as a mid-weight Euro that is not a casual affair, with a dense rulebook, long playtime and some idle time between turns, so a light social player would probably find it too heavy.

games.predicted_reason: Easy enough to teach and the trading is chatty and social, but it runs long and has some downtime and dice-luck frustration, so it stops short of a 4.
games.actual_reason: Easy to learn and sociable thanks to the trading, but the dice luck can make an unlucky night unfun and the game is middling for players wanting quick laughs.

games.predicted_reason: Taught in a minute, scales to a crowd and everyone is laughing at the clues, which hits my love of quick teaching and noise.
games.actual_reason: Learnable in minutes, scales to big groups, nobody is left out, and it produces laugh-out-loud moments, which is close to ideal for a light social player.

games.predicted_reason: Simple rules, gorgeous art and lots of chatter and laughs over the guesses, which fits my love of beautiful art and a social night.
games.actual_reason: Short rules, gorgeous art and a friendly storytelling hook make it a relaxed, social pick, though it works best with people who know each other well.

games.predicted_reason: Taught in a minute, loud, silly and tense with stick-or-twist gasps, though player elimination is a small peeve, so just under a 5.
games.actual_reason: Two-sided rules, a 15-minute length and silly humor make it a hit for casual family and friend nights, with only mild skill depth.

games.predicted_reason: Learned in a couple of minutes with short turns and pretty trains, so my low rules patience is happy, though it is a bit calm and multiplayer-solitaire.
games.actual_reason: Widely called a top gateway game that is learned in a few turns, plays in under 45 minutes, and is not stressful or confrontational.

casual.evidence_basis: Only WebSearch summaries were used (one search per game, no pages opened, BGG/Reddit blocked), so ratings rest on reviewer commentary about casual suitability rather than on confirmed casual-player posts.

games.predicted_reason: Deep, interactive and rewards mastery, but the bloated 6-8 hour endgame, kingmaking and analysis paralysis from other people hit my peeves hard.
games.actual_reason: Optimisers praise the tight strategy-card and point-track structure, but object to swingy objective draws, wildly uneven action cards, and alliance and leader-bashing politics deciding games.

games.predicted_reason: Tight tactical depth, but co-op means no real contest to win, and the long setup and rules upkeep plus fiddly rulings annoy me.
games.actual_reason: The tightly tuned tactical combat and card-economy puzzle suit optimisers, though they dislike the large class power gaps and the way solo or coordinated play makes it easier.

games.predicted_reason: Multiple routes and real skill, but it is close to multiplayer solitaire with card-draw luck and a few dominant corporations and engines.
games.actual_reason: The search summaries only gave generic praise of the engine-building and the race for finite global parameters, with nothing specific to how win-focused optimisers received it, so I can't support a rating.

games.predicted_reason: Dice and robber luck decide too many games, and kingmaking trades and runaway leaders mean a win says little about skill.
games.actual_reason: Competitive players complain that starting placement and dice luck decide too much, that trading collapses into kingmaking, and that the endgame drags into rote die rolling.

games.predicted_reason: Tense and fun, but the result rides on word-association luck and who is in the group, so skill credit is thin and it is not much of a duel.
games.actual_reason: The extra-word handicap and the risk-versus-reward clue tension read as fair and well balanced, but individual rounds swing on how easy one team's words are to clue.

games.predicted_reason: No optimal line to find and the winner is mostly subjective luck, so the result says nothing about who played better.
games.actual_reason: Reviews say competitive players find the subjective scoring too casual and the strategic depth too thin, and explicitly steer people who just want to win elsewhere.

games.predicted_reason: Nearly all luck and a take-that coin flip, so a win cannot be credited to skill, which is the Flip 7 problem.
games.actual_reason: Hobbyist reviewers dismiss it as luck-driven with early player elimination and little meaningful decision-making, so an optimiser has little to work with.

games.predicted_reason: Clean rules and a tight race with real blocking, but a dominant long-route strategy and card luck keep it below my 4 anchors.
games.actual_reason: There is real route-planning and ticket-keeping strategy to optimise, but the summaries note that ticket luck and an unavoidable luck element often outweigh skill.

competitor.evidence_basis: Only WebSearch summaries were used (one search per game, no pages opened, BGG/Reddit blocked), so ratings rest on review-site and forum summaries that mention competitive or balance concerns rather than on direct competitive-player discussion threads.
competitor.notes: Terraforming Mars rating is null (no competitor-specific evidence found), so the error is over 7 games.

games.predicted_reason: Six-plus hours and a huge rulebook the parent must master first, so it breaks my rules-simplicity and length peeves and can never be played with the kids.
games.actual_reason: Reviewers say it takes an all-day sitting with a 40-page rulebook and is aimed at 13+, so it is not realistic for casual family play unless spread over weeks.

games.predicted_reason: A thick rulebook, icon-heavy cards and campaign-length commitment make it far too hard to teach and long for a mixed-age table, though it is cooperative.
games.actual_reason: Family-oriented reviews call it overwhelming for casual families, with long setup, 2-3 hour scenarios and a campaign commitment, only working for dedicated teen-and-parent groups.

games.predicted_reason: Icon-heavy cards needing constant look-ups and a 2-hour length hit my peeves, though the theme is appealing, so it sits near Root.
games.actual_reason: One family got the basic rules after a single game, but 2-4 hour length and complexity make it a poor fit for younger kids and best for teens.

games.predicted_reason: Easy to teach in about five minutes and luck lets a child beat an adult, but trading can be harsh, a kid can fall hopelessly behind and it runs past an hour.
games.actual_reason: Families report that kids as young as nine get absorbed in the trading and luck gives younger players a chance, though it can get cutthroat.

games.predicted_reason: Rules learned in two minutes and gentle team play suit mixed ages, but a young child may struggle with the word clues and it needs enough players.
games.actual_reason: Family bloggers praise the quick rules and team play that keeps everyone in, though the spymaster role suits older kids and adults.

games.predicted_reason: Lovely art, rules taught in a minute, no take-that and a child can win, which hits nearly all my loves.
games.actual_reason: Family reviewers consistently highlight the gorgeous art, easy rules and fun across ages, with a kids version available for 6+.

games.predicted_reason: Quick rounds and trivially easy to teach with silly art, but the knock-out elimination means a child sits out, which is a peeve.
games.actual_reason: Parent reviewers like the 10-20 minute playtime, simple rules and silly cartoon tone that even a five-year-old picked up, though it is a light luck-driven elimination game.

games.predicted_reason: Learned in a round, chunky trains and a map that looks inviting, fits about 45 minutes and the luck keeps kids in the game, a true family gateway.
games.actual_reason: Searches returned only pages about the junior spin-off, Ticket to Ride First Journey, not family reception of the base game, so no supported rating.

family.evidence_basis: BoardGameGeek, reddit, wikipedia and similar were blocked and I did not open any page with WebFetch; ratings rest on WebSearch summaries of family-oriented review sites, so evidence is thin and Ticket to Ride is null because results only covered the junior spin-off.
family.notes: Ticket to Ride rating is null (only the junior spin-off was found), so the error is over 7 games.

games.predicted_reason: Factions that each tell a different story, plus table talk, betrayals and a board that collapses in memorable ways, outweigh the long rules and downtime I tolerate only at medium patience.
games.actual_reason: Reviewers describe it as a space opera where the players create a sweeping, epic narrative together, which is exactly what a story lover wants.

games.predicted_reason: A campaign where a story grows and characters change permanently is exactly what I love, though the bookkeeping and quarterbacking in co-op keep it just short of Pandemic Legacy.
games.actual_reason: Branching scenarios, story decisions with consequences and character retirement give an RPG-like campaign feel, though some reviewers call the written story a little thin.

games.predicted_reason: The theme is in the cards and the project names, but it plays like an engine-building spreadsheet with multiplayer-solitaire tendencies and heavy bookkeeping.
games.actual_reason: The theme is described as reasonably integrated and not fully pasted on, but the dated graphic design and heavy card-engine play keep immersion modest.

games.predicted_reason: Trading and the robber create some interaction and retellable moments, but the setting could be swapped for any resource game, which is my pasted-on theme peeve.
games.actual_reason: Reviewers note the theme is light and only loosely tied to the mechanics, so atmosphere-seekers find it hard to get into despite its gateway quality.

games.predicted_reason: Fun and talkative, but almost no world at all, like Flip 7, so the pasted-on spy theme earns little.
games.actual_reason: The spy theme is called pasted on and players forget it, but the social, chatty party atmosphere is still enjoyable, so a story lover finds it fine rather than loved.

games.predicted_reason: The dreamy art and the stories players tell about each card fit my love of art and retelling, though it has little rules-driven world.
games.actual_reason: Its dreamlike Marie Cardouat art and the storyteller-clue structure reward imagination and narrative creativity, a natural favourite for this type.

games.predicted_reason: Quick and silly with betrayal moments, but the cat theme is a skin and there is no world to care about, so it lands at my Flip 7 anchor.
games.actual_reason: The humorous art is charming, but reviewers call the play luck-driven and soulless, with no story or atmosphere to hold a thematic player.

games.predicted_reason: The map and train components are charming, but it is close to multiplayer solitaire where the theme could be swapped without changing play.
games.actual_reason: The nostalgic train-travel theme and chunky plastic trains charm, but reviewers say the real pull is elegant simplicity rather than story, so it is pleasant but not immersive.

story.evidence_basis: Only WebSearch summaries were used (one search per game, no pages opened, BGG/Reddit blocked), so ratings rest on review commentary about theme and story rather than on posts by self-identified thematic players.
story.notes: Largest miss: Dixit (predicted 3.5, actual 5). The profile's loves mention art and storytelling in general but give no example of an imaginative storytelling game; consider adding one at the next refresh.

games.predicted_reason: Deep multi-route planning and real interaction suit me, but the downtime, rules density and kingmaking risk (rulebook-and-AP peeves) keep it from a 5.
games.actual_reason: Heavy-strategy reviewers praise its multiple paths to victory, politics and low downtime, though the 6-8 hour length and table commitment limit how often it gets played.

games.predicted_reason: Planning card use several turns ahead is exactly the tactical depth I love, though the rulebook ambiguity, quarterbacking in co-op and some luck from modifier decks cost a point.
games.actual_reason: Reviewers highlight the card-as-health tactical puzzle and campaign decisions as deeply rewarding, which suits planners, though it is a long, heavy-setup commitment.

games.predicted_reason: I enjoy the visible engine growth and card synergies, but it leans toward multiplayer solitaire and card-draw luck decides which engines are even possible.
games.actual_reason: Its engine-building and long-term-versus-short-term planning are widely praised as strategic depth, with complaints mostly about length, card luck and component quality.

games.predicted_reason: Dice rolls undo my decisions after the fact and trading invites kingmaking and runaway leaders, which is the luck-overrides-skill peeve.
games.actual_reason: Enthusiast critics say it leans on dice luck, is simple and can outstay its welcome, and has been overtaken by less luck-driven designs, even if its trading interaction is still credited.

games.predicted_reason: Clever but a party game with little to plan, and the quarterbacking and luck of the board draw leave few decisions of my own.
games.actual_reason: Gamers say it is a smart party game that demands careful clue-giving, but it remains a light word game rather than a deep strategy one.

games.predicted_reason: There is almost nothing to plan and the winner is hard to attribute to skill, so I'm just watching the cards and votes.
games.actual_reason: Reviewers say it has little appeal to strategy fans because scoring rests on subjective interpretation rather than calculable decisions.

games.predicted_reason: Pure chance as the main event: I can't tell if I played well, which is the lowest anchor.
games.actual_reason: Hardcore-leaning reviewers call it shallow and luck-heavy, a quick funny filler with little cleverness to stand out.

games.predicted_reason: Route planning is satisfying and blocking gives some interaction, but draw luck and a mostly solved line of play make it a pleasant puzzle rather than a contest.
games.actual_reason: Seen as an excellent gateway with real route-blocking tension, but players wanting strategic depth and less luck are advised to look elsewhere.

strategist.evidence_basis: WebSearch summaries only (one search per game, not 2-3); BGG, reddit and meeplemountain are blocked and I did not open any page with WebFetch, so ratings rest on reviewer-site summaries that only partly match the heavy-gamer persona.

games.predicted_reason: Bloat is the pet peeve here: a huge rulebook and a long runtime that partly disguise kingmaking and swingy politics, though the strong faction asymmetry keeps it from a 2.
games.actual_reason: Reviewers say 4th edition trimmed the third edition's excess weight and works as a grand strategy design, though length and downtime remain standing complaints.

games.predicted_reason: The card-hand-as-resource core is a genuinely fresh decision and good play is visibly rewarded, but the bloat and fiddly setup keep it a step below a classic.
games.actual_reason: Acclaimed as a landmark campaign design (BGG about 8.8 in one summary), tempered by expert notes on fiddliness and late-campaign slog.

games.predicted_reason: Competent engine builder with real route choices, but it is familiar parts, some corporations and cards are dead picks, and the card-draw luck swings results.
games.actual_reason: Praised for card variety and theme but criticised for length, multiplayer-solitaire interaction and component or rulebook weaknesses.

games.predicted_reason: A modern classic with elegant rules and a clear shelf pitch, but I will not give it a 5 because of the trade-driven kingmaking and the dice swing.
games.actual_reason: Credited as a milestone with an exemplary short teach, while a minority of critics call the underlying design flawed (Monopoly/Risk family issues).

games.predicted_reason: One fresh, elegant decision in a rulebook that fits on a postcard, easy to pitch in one sentence, and I would defend it in any shop.
games.actual_reason: Described by reviewers as stunningly elegant and a perfect ten, with a Spiel des Jahres win and only minor spymaster-downtime gripes.

games.predicted_reason: Distinctive hook and clear teach, but the core decision is thin and not skill-driven, so it is a fine filler for the right audience.
games.actual_reason: Spiel des Jahres winner praised for simple rules and imaginative play, but I found little critical expert analysis beyond the award.

games.predicted_reason: Thin core hidden behind art and humour with swingy luck and many dead cards; it is a known shape of Russian-roulette-with-a-deck rather than new design.
games.actual_reason: Critics call it luck-driven and shallow, a triumph of branding over design, though it is accepted as a fast party filler.

games.predicted_reason: Elegant, clean rules and a clear audience with a real tension between claiming and blocking routes, only lightly solved by longest-route greed, so polish is all that is left.
games.actual_reason: Held up as an elegant gateway design with one action per turn, brisk play and low downtime, though not a deep expert favourite.

barraiser.evidence_basis: Thin: search-result summaries only; all full-article fetches were blocked by the network proxy, and BGG/Reddit were not reached. Ratings are cautious readings of expert and designer-leaning reviews.
barraiser.notes: First calibration (2026-10-03): evidence from search-result summaries only; every page read was blocked. Treat trust as provisional.

baseline_notes: The 'actual' ratings come from a first research pass that ran about one web search per game and read only search-result summaries (BoardGameGeek, Reddit, Wikipedia, Meeple Mountain and Dice Tower were blocked). Many are general reviews, not posts by players of that type.

A stricter second pass could not run: the session's 200-call web-search budget was already used up. Re-run it (ask for 'refresh the panel research') after raising the limit and allowing the blocked sites.
Two ratings are null because nothing could be supported: Terraforming Mars for the competitor, and Ticket to Ride for the family player (searches only found the junior spin-off).

The predictions were made by fresh agents shown only the persona profile, but both the predictions and the actuals draw on the same language-model knowledge of these games. Agreement shows the profiles are consistent with how a model reads the reviews; it is not independent ground truth.
The profiles were written before the actual ratings were read, and no profile was tuned after calibration (all five were within 1.0 on the first attempt).
